one_liner: A term-limited criminal investigator job at the U.S. Capitol Police for retired federal agents who already completed federal criminal investigator training and have 1811 experience.
fit_summary: Daniel does not meet the hard minimums on file. This reemployed-annuitant role requires completion of FLETC CITP, USCP BATP, or an equivalent FBI/DEA/USPIS academy, plus five years in the 1811 criminal investigator series, and nothing in Daniel's consulting or policy background supplies either. Daniel's interest in Congress and the Capitol Police is a real asset, but it is better aimed at other USCP or legislative-branch postings.
eligibility: Must have completed FLETC Criminal Investigator Training Program (CITP), USCP Basic Agent Training Program (BATP), or an equivalent FBI, DEA, or U.S. Postal Inspection Service program, and must attach the certificate or FLETC transcript.
Must have at least five years of experience in the 1811 series at the time of application; this is waived only for prior USCP employees.

The role is designed for reemployed annuitants (retired federal or law enforcement employees) on a term appointment of up to 4 years, so it is effectively limited to that group even though the hiring path says public.
You must be a U.S. citizen, under 58 at appointment, hold a REAL ID driver's license, have a high school diploma or GED, and be able to obtain and maintain a Top Secret/SCI clearance.
You must pass a polygraph, a psychological exam, a medical exam, and a full field background investigation including credit and criminal checks.
keywords: liaison with local, state, and Federal law enforcement agencies
strategy: Do not apply to this posting; without CITP/BATP training and five years of 1811 experience, the application will be screened out at the minimum-qualifications stage.

Use this posting as a signal of interest in USCP and look for its open-to-public roles instead, such as Police Officer recruit, intelligence or threat analyst, emergency management or continuity planner, and administrative or policy positions.

For USCP emergency management or planning roles, frame the IEM work around the specific preparedness, recovery, or planning tasks you performed, including the government clients involved, deliverables, and coordination with agencies, kept within two pages.
Pair the IEM experience with your knowledge of Congress and public policy to target House and Senate offices, Senate Sergeant at Arms, House Sergeant at Arms, and the Congressional Research Service.
If a sworn law enforcement career appeals to you, note that entry-level USCP Police Officer postings have different requirements; read them closely for the age limit, physical testing, and polygraph.
resume_bullets: Supported [government client] emergency preparedness efforts at IEM by [specific task, e.g., drafting plans or coordinating stakeholders], working with [number/type] federal, state, or local partners.
Prepared [type of report or assessment] identifying [risks/needs] for [client/program], which informed [decision or outcome, if known].
Served as point of contact for [stakeholder group] during [project/event], building working relationships across [agencies/offices].
interview_questions: Tell us about a time you coordinated with multiple agencies under time pressure.
How have you assessed risk or threats in your prior work, and how did you document your findings?
Why do you want to work in support of Congress specifically?
Describe a situation where you had to remain discreet with sensitive information.
watch_outs: Hard training and 1811-experience requirements make Daniel ineligible for this posting.
The role is aimed at retirees on a term appointment of up to 4 years and is not a career entry point.
The job requires shift work 24/7 including nights, weekends, and holidays, along with firearm proficiency, a polygraph, and a TS/SCI clearance.
Travel for hiring assessments and training is at the applicant's expense.
